Cfjrtgtmasi Creese 

When you think of Christmas trees 
What^do you recall? 

Do you see them piled on city lots 
Or leaned against a wall? 

Are they tagged for busy shoppers. 

Who know not spruce from pine. 

Nor ever guess the long slow years 
To make a tree’s design? 

When you think of Christmas trees 
Are they in some heated place. 

Standing in the corner 

Of a gaily-cluttered space; 

Hung witth loops of tinsel 
And bulbs of colored light, 

Weighed down with parcels 
Wrapped in papers bright? 

When 7 think of Christmas trees 
I see them where they grow 
Out in the forests 

Standing in the snow; 

Dark spires against the sky 
Draped in frosty frills 
Shining in the moonlight 
Out on the hills. 

When I think of Christmas trees 
Glowing gems are there 
Glistening on the branches 
In the cold night air. 

They seem to reach so very high 
Above the snow-clad sod, 

Up, and ever up, they point 
Above the stars, to God, 

, —Mary S. Edgar 

With every good wish to our readers for Christmas and the New Year

Creatimtyi 

in Cunudiun I^ife * 


The Massey Report on National 
Development in Art, Letters and 
Sciences and its accompanying volume 
of special studies is a thoughtful mas¬ 
terpiece of charm, wisdom and design 
wherein the potentialities of the Cana¬ 
dian life have been brought to light 
and carefully assayed. This magnifi¬ 
cent document presents a definite chal¬ 
lenge to leaders in youth organizations 
and will bring pleasure and stimulus \o 
even the casual reader. 

The underlying thesis of the Report 
is that the good things of the mind, 
from scholarship to handicrafts, from 
Indian arts to town planning, must 
have greater support. Through the 
ages they have existed, for the most 
part, under some form of patronage 
but if they are to flourish increasingly 
Government sources, both Federal and 
Provincial, must give greater concern 
and increased financial support. As' a 
nation we have pas.sed the pioneer 
period and today there is 
a growing interest in cultural pursuits. 
This is evident in an increased library 
circulation and the opening of new 
libraries in rural communities, heavier 
enrolment in night classes, greater in¬ 
terest in Museums, Art GallerVs and 
exhibitions such as the Viennese Col¬ 
lection. There has been remarkable 


growth in rhusic, drama and handicraft 
organizations. The number of small 
town barids is impressive and plays 
and operettas are no longer confined 
to the larger centres. Furthermore the 
recent changes in working conditions 
have made provision for greater leisure, 
for both white collar and factory work¬ 
ers, resulting in greater opportunity to 
follow cultural pursuits. Wood carvers, 
handicraft workers ^nd amateur paint¬ 
ers are showing their skills and their 
colours everyw^hcre. 

It would appear, therefore, that the 
trend to greater government concern 
and increased government support is 
not only justifiable but also inevitable. 

The recommendations of the Massey 
Report are based on the implicit 
assumption that there are rich veins 
of potential creativity within our na¬ 
tional groups. The Report also assumes 
that new life infused into these groups 
will bring forth a great flowering of 
that creativity. However, only with 
full cooperation and support from Gov¬ 
ernment as well as from humanitarian 
and social organizations, will that flow¬ 
ering wax more glorious as the years 
roll by and become for all the diversi¬ 
fied peoples of our broad Dominion ‘a 
thing of beauty and a joy forever’. 


Toronto^ Canada^'December, 1951 


7 



Another factor that will be of ines¬ 
timable value in bringing about this 
flowering will come through intelligent 
and enthusiastic leadership. Leadership 
quick to recognize stirrings of creative¬ 
ness, leadership with personality and 
power to develop confidence, leadership 
with knowledge of how to direct that 
creative trend and bring the latent tal¬ 
ent to a measure of fulness. It is at this 
point that leaders, having discovered 
veins of creativity, find themselves han¬ 
dicapped. The road to achievement is 
difficult and costly. Low-priced materi¬ 
als and training centres are not avail¬ 
able in most centres; the same is true 
of stimulus in the way of monetary 
grants and scholarships. It is in this 
direction that government aid can be 
of great value. It will also bear fruit 
by creating a happy (rather than a 
frustrated) state of mind in individuals 
who have been led to believe that they 
have creative ability. This, therefore, 
will make for good citizenship as well 
as good artistry. 

Children, even at a very early age, 
must be given encouragement to ex¬ 
press their creative tendencies. They 
must have free play to work out the 
ideas which flash into their minds and 
when something appears to them to 
have value or beauty their desire for 
expression must be met with a sym¬ 
pathy which will lead them to trust 
their own intuitions. In the nursery, 
in the home, in the school, in summer 
camps and in youth organizations, there 
must be this atmosphere of under¬ 
standing and cooperation which - will 
fan the flame of expression. This will 
be to vouth as sunshine is to growing 
plants. They will then paint as they 
see things, they will work out little 
rhyme patterns and song and dance 
rhythms (and when they are older, 
short stories and poetic stanzas). They 
will dramatize, and with amazing 
reality; even shy individuals, playing 
at charades, will act parts with remark¬ 
able savoir faire. Having been given 


encouragement in creative activities 
and having had no cause to fear the 
public opinion bogey they will con¬ 
tinue to find great delight, as they 
grow up, in these activities. They will 
also discover that there is not only a 
thrill but also satisfying reward in 
‘being creative*. Public approval, prizes 
and other incentives (though they may 
stimulate effort and strengthen confi¬ 
dence) will become, as they should, of 
secondary value. 

At the same time youth must learn 
that artistry, like citizenship, demands 
controls. As citizens we must conform 
to traffic regulations and to many other 
controls which put the brakes on un¬ 
limited freedom of expression. Good 
artistry makes the same demands. 
Care must be taken not to ruin the 
desired effect by exaggeration; restraint 
must be exercised to keep the story or 
the painting from being cluttered. Fine 
work of any kind calls for habitual 
controls: patient effort, honesty and 
integrity of execution. 

This method of education will de¬ 
velop imagination and ingenuity. It 
will also make for independence of 
thought and action and, to a certain 
extent, should counteract the present 
trend of running, willy-nilly, with the 
crowd, like sheep. 

The Massey Report is a Canadian 
Report: its studies are of Canadian 
life and literature; its recommendations 
are for Canadian people. There is 
much in it, for old and young, ‘to read, 
mark and inwardly digest*. Though 
young children may not be able to 
grasp the concept of Canada as a 
political and economic unit we must 
help them as they grow to maturity 
to know, understand and love this 
land of ours. From our well-grounded 
fear of Jingoism we have sometimes 
forgotten to make our children con¬ 
scious of the wonderful heritage that 
is theirs. They must realize that they 


8 


Canadian Camping 



belong to a country whose history^ 
though short, is thrilling, whose 
resources are tremendous, whose coun¬ 
tryside in all its diversity has strength, 
colour and grandeur, and whose future 
promises security and prosperity. 

It will take years to grasp what is 
behind all this but each year our chil¬ 
dren must learn something more about 
our forests, our waterways, our wheat 
fields, our rich oil deposits—the roots 
from which our Canadian life and com¬ 
merce grow. That their imaginations 
may be stirred we must help them to 
visualize this Canada of ours. Films, il¬ 
lustrated lectures and radio presenta¬ 
tions all have a great part to play. Spe¬ 
cially planned trips for children, where 
they will become acquainted with our 
great waterways, our wilderness forest 
areas, our systems of water storage 
constructed to make electricity, — all 
these present wonderful opportunities 
to study the underlying structure of our 
natural resources. At summer camps 
and cottages children should be en¬ 
couraged to explore the background of 
that part of Canada where they happen 
to be. Too often families holidaying in 
the wilds bring with them the devastat¬ 
ing attitudes of city life—hurry, competi¬ 
tion and artificial sociability and there 
is no time to enjoy and get the feel of 
the out-of-doors. Surely to follow the 
courses of the streams that enter ‘our’ 
lake, to paddle quietly along the shore, 
learning something about the trees and 
the birds and the animal life of the 
woodland is a vital experience which 
is worth more than making a speed boat 
record. Experiences of this kind leave 
a deep impression and often change 
the whole course of one’s life. If our 
children can come to realize the glory 
and beauty of tiiese contacts they will 
experience the growing delight and 
deep-seated satisfaction, trip after trip 
and season after searor, of adding to 
their store of knov/ledge of the out-of- 
doors. Following this way of life they 


Toronto, Canada, December, 1951 


will also learn something about the 
stream sources of our Canadian spirit, 

Wc become truly Canadian only as 
we learn to know and understand and 
love Canada, As parents and teachers, 
leaders and friends of youth, it is our 
responsibility so to guide our youth 
that they, too, will know and under¬ 
stand and love Canada. If we can 
accomplish something in this direction, 
year after year, the recommendations 
of the Massey Report will soon have 
become part and parcel of our Cana¬ 
dian life. That flowering of creativity 
will have ushered in a new era. 

The following remarks, quoted from 
an address given by His Excellency the 
Governor-General, as he opened the 
1951 sale of contemporary painting held 
recently at the Art Gallery in Toronto 
are in line with the dominating themes 
of the Massey Report. “History shows 
that, as new countries grow and de¬ 
velop, they tend to express their nation¬ 
al characteristics through the Arts. In 
the world of painting Canada has al¬ 
ready struck out on a line which is both 
original and distinctive. Eventually 
Canada will give to the world, in other 
fields of cultural pursuits, contrbutions 
which can be labelled as distinctly 
Canadian.” 

*The greater part of this article has 
been worked out from one written by 
Dr. Mary L. Northway for the Bulletin 
of the Institute of Child Study. Con¬ 
siderable abridgment has been neces¬ 
sary and certain additions have been 
made to adapt it to the point of view of 
the readers of Canadian Camping.

John Hoyle 

Director: Gay Venture Camp 
President: Ontario Camping Association 


The adequate training of the camp 
staff is one of the most urgent prob¬ 
lems facing a camp director. It is a 
never-ending problem because due to 
the vagaries of life, counsellors of this 
season may be nurses-in-training, insur¬ 
ance clerks, or maybe even entering the 
halcyon gates of matrimony, by next 
summer. 

While it is not impossible, it is diffi¬ 
cult to give cabin counsellors any kind 
of adequate training during the camp 
season. Their day is so replete that 
they need every moment of their daily 
period off duty for relaxation, and when 
evening comes and their duties are over 
for the day, minds and bodies are tired 
and hardly in .a receptive mood for 
concentrated thought and the alertness 
of mind required for either lecture or 
discussion. For these reasons, while not 
by any means neglecting entirely the in¬ 
camp training, we have found it exped*- 
ent to concentrate training primarily 
on the pre-counsellor-age girl. 

There is, however, another reason for 
this emphasis. Young people of to-day 
mature socially earlier than they did a 
generation ago. It has been our experi¬ 
ence that at sixteen and seventeen years 
of age young people are saying some¬ 
thing like this: “I have been a camper 
for seven or eight years. I have com¬ 
pleted satisfactorily all the available 
tests in camp activities. I feel I am 
ready to become a cabin counsellor 
and share my learnings and experience 
with younger campers.” 


This altruistic attitude, for that is 
what it is basically, is typical of a great 
number of girls who are looking for a 
place where they may share their ex¬ 
perience with those their chronological 
juniors. Of course the motivat'ons un-. 
derlying this attitude'are complex and 
space does not permit "a discussion of 
them here. The fact remains that these 
young people are saying: “Here we 
are; we are ready for service. If you 
do not wish to use us we shall be com¬ 
pelled to look elsewhere.” And why 
should we lose the services of these 
charming, experienced (in skills) and 
socially-minded people? 

Aware of this challenging situation 
a plan to meet it was proposed a few 
years ago. It is really a five-year plan. 
While not yet adequate and while sub¬ 
ject to change as we become aware of 
better ways of doing things it is point¬ 
ing the way to better days ahead. The 
emphasis is at present on the sixteen and 
seventeen year old girls. However, we 
start work on the fourteen-year-olds in 
an introductory manner. 

Here is the plan: Girls of fourteen 
and fifteen years of age who show lead¬ 
ership-potential are enrolled, if they 
volunteer, in our Leadership Training 
Plan. During the season these girls meet 
three or four times with the camp direc¬ 
tor who devotes more than half of his 
daily schedule to leadership* education 
and personality guidance. At these ses¬ 
sions these girls are presented'with the 
challenge, opportunity, and sacrifice of 


10 


Canadian Camping 



leadership through camp counselling. 
This is correlated with experience by 
giving them the opportunity of under¬ 
takings according to their ability, cer¬ 
tain actual leadership skills. These 
might include putting, a cabin group 
of young children to bed, telling stories, 
taking charge of a table in the dining 
room, working out, and on, some pro¬ 
ject for improving the camp site, or 
taking charge of a small group in some 
craft activity. 

Let us take the technique employed 
in putting a cabin group to bed as 
representative of other similar activities. 
The Camper in training is assigned first 
to spend an evening observing a coun¬ 
sellor as she puts a group to bed. On 
the second night she helps the counsel¬ 
lor, and in doing so (we hope) she 
assimilates something of the counsellor's 
technique. After the campers are asleep 
she discusses the methods used with the 
counsellor. For the following two 
nights (making four nights in all) the 
roles are reversed and the young lady 
in training takes charge of putting the 
cabin group to bed, with the counsellor 
remaining in the background. Follow¬ 
ing “goodnight” the two confer. The 
tramee may ask explanation of this or 
that method and the counsellor may 
suggest how the trainee might have 
handled one or more situations in a 
more effective way. 

It should be understood clearly that 
the girls who enroll in this preliminary 
training program of leadership are not 
counsellors in training but are merely 
senior girls who are seized with the urge 
to leadership. This elementary part of 
our training program is still very much 
in the experimental stage but the ex¬ 
perience we have had so far indicates 
that the project has very real values 
and that it more than justifies the very 
considerable time and thought devoted 
to it. Not only does the experience give 


an added zest to a camper of many 
years who may be getting a little dis¬ 
satisfied with ordinary camper activities 
but it also gives the camp director some 
indications of the effectiveness of the 
camp program as well as the potential 
leadership available for the future. 

At sixteen a girl, if she meets the 
requirements of the camp, may enroll 
as a junior counsellor in training. If, 
in this role, she completes the summer 
with a successful record she may be 
invited to return the. following year as 
a senior G.I.T. If as a junior or a 
senior G.I.T. her record is not up to 
requirements she may be asked to re¬ 
peat her year. Naturally, some do not 
wish to do this. Where a girl does so 
our records show that one hundred per 
cent make good. In other words, when 
a girl shows the necessary strength of 
character to be willing to repeat her 
year she has later become a successful 
counsellor. 

A counsellor in training is not a 
“Jo-girl”. She is always treated as a 
leader-in-traming. True, she may be 
asked to help counsellors in clearing 
away the tables in the Lodge for an 
evening programme or in collecting 
wood for a staff party but these arc, 
after all, part of training. The whole 
emphasis is on learning how to become 
a leader through mental and physical 
experience. 

A junior counsellor in training takes 
part in the four daily programme peri¬ 
ods. For one of these periods she is 
definitely assigned to a discussion group 
conducted by the director. This takes 
the form of a discussion-lecture group 
designed for the purpose of helping a 
girl to understand herself. As a basic 
guide the textbook “Towards the Un¬ 
derstanding of Youth” by the writer, 
and published by the Ganadian Gouncil 
of Ghurches, is used. Through the 
medium of the ten chapters written in 


Toronto^ Canada^ December^ 1951 


11 



everyday language the student acquires 
a simple but comprehensive understand¬ 
ing of her relationship to the forces of 
heredity, plus the influences and adjust¬ 
ments of home, school, church, friends 
and community. The course might well 
be described as ‘‘An orientation course 
for youth.” The first question asked 
each morning is “has anything occurred 
in camp since we last met that you 
would like to discuss?” Thanks to the 
mutual confidence that exists between 
Gs.I.T. and leader, several questions are 
usually raised regarding various be¬ 
haviour problems and the methods used 
in meeting them, the reason for some 
new regulation, the lack of interest 
in some activity, or the interest or 
otherwise in ,some special day pro¬ 
gramme. The Gs.I.T. appreciate the 
freedom and understanding of this 
period, and incidentally, it gives the 
director a marvellous insight into the 
working of the camp as seen bv fifteen 
or twenty alert, keen and critical young 
people. Experience has shown that the 
mutual confidences in this group are 
never abused. 

If properly qualified a junior G.LT. 
will assist for one period a day as a 
life-guard. She may devote the other 
two periods to developing her own per¬ 
sonal skills or, if qualified, may assist 
in the instruction of some skill under 
the supervision of a counsellor. We do 
say this to our junior Gs.I.T. “This is 
the last summer when you will have 
much freedom in selecting your activi¬ 
ties. Think well over the skills in which 
you are weak and plan to improve them 
this season. By all means emphasize the 
skills in which you are particularly 
interested but plan to be at least moder¬ 
ately good in all camp activities. Try 
and plan to be an all-round counsellor 
prepared to give leadership wherever 
you may be needed.” 

The senior counsellor in training 
(seventeen years of age) also attends a 


daily discussion period with the direc¬ 
tor. The content of this course deals 
with the camp philosophy to which 
much time is devoted. This is due to 
our feeling that no leadership can be 
adequate unless the philosophy under¬ 
lying all the camp objectives, methods 
and programme are clearly understood 
and accepted. The camp philosophy is 
correlated with a study of the technique 
of understanding campers’ behaviour 
both as individuals and in their group 
relationships; methods of meeting suc¬ 
cessfully behaviour problems: sugges¬ 
tions and practise in story-telling, pre¬ 
paring a service of worship, etc.; the 
meaning and technique of leadership 
and a study of all camp relationships 
such as camper-counsellor, counsellor- 
counsellor, counsellor r administration. 
Daily opportunity is also given here for 
a consideration of the why and where- 
for of the daily happenings in camp. 

Theoretically a senior counsellor in 
training has one free period a day simi¬ 
lar to the counsellors’ perod off for 
relaxation. In this period she may pre¬ 
fer to participate in some activity or 
she may use it for a conference with 
the director or the programme director. 
For the remaining two periods the 
senior G.I.T. is assigned to activities 
where she may assist the counsellors in 
their activities, and develop her skills 
in coaching through experience. For 
the past two or three years, however, 
senior Gs.I.T. have asked that they be 
not given a period off as they would 
prefer to be assigned to some activity. 
This rather interesting request has been 
granted. 

Every two weeks or so the director 
receives a report on every G.I.T. from 
all Section Heads and Activity Heads 
with whom she has worked. A schedule 
is then set up and the director spends 
from twenty minutes to half an hour 
with each G.I.T. discussing with her 
these reports and together discovering 


12 


Canadian Gam ping 



ways in which any weaknesses reported 
upon may be faced and conquered. The 
value of these individual conferences is 
incalculable. 

Last year, for the first time, a senior 
staff member was appointed to give a 
large portion of her time to actually 
supervising the counsellors in training in 
their activities, making sure that they 
are getting every opportunity for coach¬ 
ing and assisting them in their several 
teaching techniques. This staff member 
also functioned as the G.I.T. Advisor 
and the relationships established in that 
way were definitely valuable. 

So far we have referred briefly to 
four years of training. Under this plan 
a girl who has completed her service as 
a senior counsellor in training may be 
invited to return as a cabin counsellor, 
or she may, if she wishes, apply for a 
position in some other camp. We are 
quite alive to the fact that the average 
eighteen year old girl is not sufficiently 
emotionally mature to be given full 
charge of a cabin group. We feel we 
are really asking too much of them. 
Before too long we hope to raise the 
minimum age to nineteen. 


It is also evident that despite all the 
training these Gs.I.T. have had in 
leadership and skills the actual cabin 
group responsibility brings not only 
much greater responsibility than was 
anticipated but presents problems 
hitherto not actually experienced. -For 
this reason we are endeavouring to 
work out a plan to continue the train¬ 
ing for this age group. While we have 
not yet found the answer to any form 
of group training we have emphasized 
that both the director and the pro¬ 
gramme director are always available 
for conference—they are never too busy 
to'confer with counsellors on their prob¬ 
lems. This attitude has been recognized 
and is appreciated. Every day there 
are numerous such conferences and it 
may be that more worthwhile results 
can be secured in this way than through 
a more formal discussion group. 

In evaluating this training pro¬ 
gramme which is experimental and in¬ 
complete we can report that counsellors 
who have followed it through have 
almost invariably turned out to be our 
most reliable, understanding and effec¬ 
tive staff members. 


From the farewell speech of H.R.H. Princess Elizabeth 


I thank you for the glimpse you have given me of the 
greatness of this nation and the even greater future which is 
within its grasp. 

1 have seen this future in the eyes of hundreds of thousands 
of your children and have heard it in their voices. For as long 
as 1 live I shall 'remember and cherish fondly the greetings 
which came to us each day from those young people. I pray 
that their lot in this land ivill always continue to he a happy one.

Something had to be about 

‘nature’ in our camp.-, Jfere we were 
living in the great.j oi 4 t-of-doors and 
knowing and caring'so little about our 
out-door neighbors! 

We had' tried classes and* interest 
groups in other seasons and had'failed 
miserably. We had the necessary books 
in the reference library but they re¬ 
mained unopened. Occasionally a ‘bom 
nature lover’ would stop to look at 
something; outside of that we had little 
time for such things. 

. We made a discovery, however, and 
found that we made much more pro¬ 
gress in this direction when we learned 
to recognize the ‘leads’ which the camp¬ 
ers themselves offered us and how best 
to make use of them. We also secured 
information regarding experiments be¬ 
ing made by Mr. Ellsworth Jaeger in a 
Nature Day Gamp in cqnnection with 
the Buffalo Museum of Natural History. 

At their weekly camp fire each camper 
wore a felt shoulder belt andy as he was 
able to identify‘flowers, birds,'animals, 
etc., he was given an appropriate sym¬ 
bol to wear on it. We decided to ti'y 
that, adding some camp craft as well 
(choosing wood for fires/ building fires, 
simple cooking). Definite periods were 
set aside when the juniors could ‘explore 
and practise with adult assistance. This 


• i • 

fifii, 


scheme proved most successful and pro¬ 
fitting by Mr. Jaeger’s findings no more 
than five new species were to be identi¬ 
fied on any one trip. The juniors loved 
their camp fires, with their own fire¬ 
lighting ritual, their own songs, nature 
stories and games. 

Following up the ‘leads’ of the older 
campers was more difficult and one 
really needed a museum staff to deal 
with them. One, for instance; WAs a 
tin half full of sand. “We’re sure there’s 
gold in it. Couldn’t we have it ana¬ 
lyzed?” What* a jumping-off‘place for 
awakening an interest in geology! Btit 
no member of the staff was able to 
help and our reference books were quite 
inadequate. The next ‘lead’ was a 
raccoon. She haunted our garbage pails 
and one day upset the can and covered 
herself with beet juice, leaving her trail 
as she made a tour of the verandah. 
Everyone became interested in raccoons 
but being a night visitor it was almost 
impossible to get a good look at her and 
she was very shy after she had a litter 
of five little ones. 

Nature hikes as such were usually out, 
but a hike to pick raspberries or to visit 
the fire warden’s tower was fun and 
trips and picnics and hikfes were made 
occasions, by counsellor's as well as 
campers, of identifying "“five species

(birds, flowers, trees, etc ), softietimes 
a first five, .sometiitnes‘ a second. • An 
interesting detail about each’one helped 
to make the identification more perma¬ 
nent: White Pine, five letters, five 
needles; shinleaf, used by Indians for 
medicinal purposes; spruce, provides a 
gum which can be used for mending 
a canoe; vireos, always^ decorate their 
nests. Several natural phenomena were 
exciting enough to write home about: 
a beaver dam, a colourful display of 
Northern Lights, and an eclipse of the 
moon. Late hours may have had some¬ 
thing to do with the last two. 

Constant use was made of posters. 
They were simple and gay with colour 
and the print was large enough to read 
with ease. With posters for birds there 
were spaces for listing the species, where 
they had been seen, and the names of 
campers who had spotted" them. Col¬ 
oured pictures of birds were often used 
to illustrate them. With flower or weed 
posters real specimens were used. 


Team games (four or five minute 
periods) were played imthe diningrbom, 
table againsf'table. “Victims” would He 
selected ^d.* then the' annouri’cem’ent 
would be made: “Wanted:, a basswood 
seed' . .^a hemlbek cone’ . . . two 

different pietes of birch'bark.” 

We experimented with making fires. 
Four fires, as near in size as possible, 
were built on the same plan;'one with 
soft wood,* another with driftwood, the 
third with'birch'and a little kindling, 
the fourth'with* maple. They were light¬ 
ed at the same moment. A few minutes 
later, the canfper designated who 
touched The cold ashes of the soft wood 
arid inlmedfately afterwards the ashes of 
the maple suffered* a painful surprise! 

Many of the campers went home 
from .camp wearing their shoulder belts 
resplendent with insignia. One way and 
another awareness of the out-of-door 
world h,ad made itself felt in the con¬ 
sciousness of J:he campers, and to our 
great delight, of the counsellors as well.

15 



British Columhia 
Camp Roundup 

The first fall meeting of the B.C. 
Branch, Canadian Camping Associa¬ 
tion, was held in a lounge of the 
Y.M.C.A. Our president, Phyllis Porter, 
had changed her name to Phyllis Robin¬ 
son during the summer, and everyone 
agreed that she had had the most suc¬ 
cessful holiday. 

The fact that there had been not a 
drop of rain throughout the camping 
season this year made out-door sports, 
especially swimming, the highlight of 
the summer. It even curtained to some 
extent trips to the woods because of 
fire restrictions, but everyone agreed 
these restrictions were easier to cope 
with than rainy days at Camp. 

The Stratford Children’s Camp at 
Roberts Creek had a very successful 
season, which Mrs. Galliford reported 
due to good leadership. A Red Cross 
Course in swimming and life saving 
gave her counsellors an opportunity to 
carry through a very pertinent program 
of waterfront safety. 

The Zionist Camp at Crescent Beach, 
now in its 15th year, had a staff of 17. 
Children from 9-17 came from all over 
B.C. and from the Western States to 
work and play together in a program 
of appreciation of their racial back¬ 
ground and its contribution to the com¬ 
munity as a whole. 

In-City Camping was carried out by 
the Y.M.C.A. in Boys’ Town during 
the summer. Mr. Allan Wooten report¬ 
ed that the B.C. Natural History Society 
arranged Woodland Rambles, Beach 
trips and trips to the Zoo and the Agri¬ 
cultural College where the boys re¬ 
ceived first hand instruction from lead¬ 
ers in the field. 

Camp Fircom, the First United 
Church Camp on Howe Sound, was a 
busy place this summer. Deaconess M. 
Richardson reported many mothers 
and young children attended and many 


more 7-8 year olds without mothers. 
There were the usual Explorer Groups 
and the Hi Y campers. 

Miss Gertrude Moore agreed that the 
summer was perfect for the swimming 
and boating program at Moorcroft. 
Her campers enjoyed sleeping outdoors 
but due to the dryness of the woods they 
did have to keep to main highways and 
missed their outdoor cooking sprees. 
Birds were very plentiful around Moor¬ 
croft, especially since their water tank 
overflowed, and the children learned 
to identiy many small birds. 

Children’s Jubilee Summer Camp, 
situated on the North Arm of Burrard 
Inlet which, since 1935, has been oper¬ 
ated by the Trade Unions, Fraternal 
Women’s Organization, was reported 
by Mrs. Cook and Mrs. Ford. Here 
leadership is voluntary. The slogan for 
their camp is “Campers to-day, leaders 
to-morrow”. 

Charlie Roche of Camp Howdy re¬ 
ported about his camping experiences 
in his native land, Australia, where 
camping is carried on by the govern¬ 
ment on a 12 month basis, and is a 
part of the school curriculum. This 
summer he made a tour through the 
United States and Eastern Canada, vis¬ 
iting camps of many different types. 
Here he picked up many new ideas, saw' 
camps which impressed him very much 
and other camps which he felt were 
losing some of the spontaneous natural 
setting of true camping experience. 
Indeed, we learned about leadership 
training camps, something of how mir¬ 
aculously 300 campers would be fed 
and all traces of the meal disposed of 
within twenty minutes. We had a good 
laugh over some of his experiences in 
a very posh Girl’s Camp when a group 
of boys got shipwrecked off their beach, 
and we were quite intrigued over the 
program of instruction in the ways of 
Emily Post at a Welfare Camp in the 
Eastern States. 

So ended our first round-up of the 
year. 


16 


Canadian Camping 


A Greeting 
to O.A.C. Members 

This Fall, in deep humility, I step 
into the office of President of the On¬ 
tario Camping Association, a position 
so admirably filled by Mr. Ted Yard 
for the past two years. 

This is not the place to discuss details 
of plans for the future, but may I take 
this opportunity of making one observa¬ 
tion? It is only as we place our major 
emphasis on character, on personality 
development, on guiding thinking to¬ 
wards that kind of living that is rich 
and abundant and reaching out that 
camping may be considered to be worth 
the time, money, and effort put into it. 
Gamp activities, skills and programme 
are all a “must” but their permanent 
value lies only in the contribution they 
make to Canadian citizenship on the 
highest level. 

Stanley Jones in “The Way to Power 
and Poise” refers to a definition of 
democracy which states “Democracy is 
that madness which believes about peo¬ 
ple that which isn’t true, and yet with¬ 
out that belief they will never become 
what we believe them to be.” Change 
that word Democracy to Camping and 
read it again. You now have a defini¬ 
tion with power to revolutionize much 
of our camping philosophy and pro¬ 
gramme. Will you read it again and 
think it over in light of your own camp 
objectives? It’s dynamite, it’s T.N.T.— 
in fact, it’s atomic. 

John Hoyle. 



- Toronto, Canada^ December^ 1951 


THE CANADIAN NATIONAL 
INSTITUTE FOR THE BLIND 

. . . operated Gamps in three provinces 
last summer. Sunshine Gamp at Sooke, 
18 miles from Victoria, B.C., was held 
for the twelfth season. Dry weather 
and strict forestry regulations made pic¬ 
nics off the premises impossible last 
summer, but sea bathing and sun bath¬ 
ing on the beach, with many other hap¬ 
py activities, filled the Gamp days for 
the thirty-two campers. Manitoba’s 
first Camp was on Lake Winnipeg’s 
western shore. “Best vacation since 
losing our sight” was the unanimous 
comment. Ancaster, Ontario, reached 
an all-time high in attendance, which 
was 183. Some of the Campers took 
their Red Gross Swimming Tests. Han¬ 
dicrafts were popular with over 40 in 
one period. Busy days and interesting 
evenings resulted in growth and devel¬ 
opment which could be observed daily. 


Sn iHemoriam 

« 

The Ontario Camping Associa¬ 
tion sustained a great loss in the 
death on October 25th of Mrs. 
Joseph Danson, one of the Charter 
Members and a former member 
of the Board. 

Mrs. Danson' was director of 
Gamp Winnebagoe in Muskoka, 
which was established in 1933. 
She had a warm, understanding 
personality, which won her a wide 
circle of loyal friends. 

Our sympathy goes out to all 
the members of her family, three 
of whom, her husband, her son 
William, and her daughter Mari¬ 
lyn, have rendered valuable ser¬ 
vice as board members of O.G.A.

TThe JBirthiright (Child>rem 


All children should know the jay of playing in healthful mud^ 
of paddling in clean water, of hearing birds sing praises to God 
for the new day. 

They should have the vision of pure skies enriched at dawn 
and sunset ^with unspeakable glory; of dew drenched mornings 
flashing with priceless gems; of the vast sky all throbbing and 
panting with stars. 

They should live with flowers and butterflies, with the wild 
things that have made possible the world of fables. 

They should experience the thrill of going barefoot, of being 
out in the rain; of riding a white birch, of sliding down pine 
boughs, of climbing ledges and tsSl trees, of diving head-first into* 
a transparent pool. 

They ought to know the smell of the wet earth, of new mown 
hay, of sweet fern mint, and, fir; of the breath of cattle and of 
fog blown inland from the sea. 

They should hear the answer the trees make to the ram and 
to the wind; the sound of rippling and falling water; the muffled 
roar of the sea in storm. 

They should have a chance to fish, to ride on a load of hay, 
to camp out, cook over an open fire, tramp through a new country 
and sleep under the open sky. 

■ They should have the fun of riding a horse, paddling a canoe, 
sailing a boat. . . 

One cannot appreciate and enjoy to the full extent nature, 
books, novels, histories, poems, pictures, or even musical composi¬ 
tions, who has not in his youth enjoyed the blessed contact with 
the world of nature. 

—Henry Turner Bailey 
(from Camping Magazine)

Book Beviews 


HOLIDAY GRAFT AND FUN by 
Joseph Leeming. Longmans’ Green 
& Go. Obtainable in Canada from 
G. R. Welch Co., 1149 King St. W., 
Toronto. Price $3.25. 

This book is crammed with illustra¬ 
tions and descriptions of clever things 
children can make_, such as invitations, 
favours, decorations, and appropriate 
games for special occasions. It is a gold 
mine of ideas for camp, school and 
home parties—^ideas that can be easdv 
and inexpensively carried out by boys 
and girls. 

FUN WITH FABRICS by Joseph 
Learning. Longmans’ Green & Co. 
Obtainable in Canada from G. R. 
Welch Go., 1149 King St. W., Toron¬ 
to. Price $3.25. 

This is another clever book by the 
same author. It is full of amusing and 
suggestive ideas about things to make 
from cloth,and felt, and it is profusely 
illustrated. It is a fabric book for boys 
as well as girls, which seems unusual, 
but it includes scores of fascinating 
things that boys can make for them¬ 
selves, such as a pup tent, signal flags, 
a fabric surf-board and a ship’s ham-j 
mock. There are also many purely 
feminine articles that girls will love to 
make in the craft-shop at Gamp.

MEASURE OF THE YEAR by Roder¬ 
ick Haig-Brown Collins. 1950. 279 
pages. 

“Measure of the Year” should be 
compulsory reading for Camp Direc¬ 
tors. It is delightful. Canada, through 
the year, as it is reflected in Nature and 
in life, is the. theme. Conservation, 
Children, Gardens, Trees, Visitors, 
Woods, Libraries, Hunting and Canada 
are among the subjects. It is a book to 
be digested, but sipped slowly as rare, 
mellow wine. Its chapters ask to be 
read aloud by our winter firesides. The 
only disadvantage to its being read 
aloud is that the reader will be inter¬ 
rupted frequently with “that reminds 
me . . . !” or “I’ve so often thought 
that, but never thought of saying it 
just that way ” M.L.N. 


HUNDREDS OF THINGS A BOY 
CAN MAKE. Published by The 
Musson Book Company Ltd., To¬ 
ronto. Price $1.25. 

The sub-title of this book is “a hobby 
book for boys of all ages,” and it is 
indeed just that. There is a great deal 
in this book to attract and interest the 
average boy. With a copy at his elbov/ 
he would never be at a loss to know 
how to spend his time. There are in¬ 
numerable paragraphs describing the 
making of toys, there are directions on 
the construction of useful articles fof 
the home, and there are descriptions of 
things to make for bazaars and sales 
of work. It is a guide and reference 
book to turn to on a hundred occasions.

PAPER-BAG AND 
PAPER-PLATE MASKS 


From one of the books reviewed in ^ 
diis issue, “Holiday Craft and Fun”, 
there are simple directions for making 
%-arious types of masks. With paper 
hags you can make dozens of different 
kinds of faces with pencil, crayons or 
paint. You can paste on crepe-paper 
hair, eyebrows, ears or whiskers of 
coloured construction paper. Cut holes 
in the bag for eyes, nose and mouth. 
Clever masks can also be made quickly 
and easily by using paper plates. Draw 
eyes, nose and mouth on the outside of 
the plate. Gut these out with the point 
of a knife or scissors, then decorate with 
crayons, adding eyebrows, hair, etc. 
Make two small holes on each side of 
the rim and attach a piece of string 
through the holes for tying around the 
bead. Campers could give their imagi¬ 
nations full rein. 

SPAGHETTI SAUCE 

When a case of gallon-size tins of 
Spaghetti Sauce arrived in Gamp last 
summer, instead of the smaller case of 
23-oz. tins which we had anticipated, 
oar first impulse was to promptly ship 
it back, but the Dietitian suggested we 
sample it. It was not long before we 
were ready to order another case. One 
of the recipes which proved most popu¬ 
lar with the campers was meat-balls 
with Spaghetti and Spaghetti Sauce, 
and this was discovered to be an excel¬ 
lent way to use left-over meat. Corn 
beef loaf with the sauce was also popu¬ 
lar. Spaghetti Sauce is tasty and eco¬ 
nomical and is available from our 
a<h*ertisers, Gumpert Go., Ltd., who 
will also provide you with some excel¬ 
lent recipes.

In Liffhtftr Vein 

Once there was a Camper 
At Camp-Craft she excelled 
Kabohs and stews were specialties 
Her puddings always jelled. 

She learned the art of building fires, 
The kind of wood to choose, 

The surest way to pitch a tent 
The sort of axe to use. 

Back home in town, when camp was 
done 

Of all her skills she’d boast: 

Her family grew skeptical. 

For she burned the morning toast! 

The human brain is a Wonderful thing. 
It starts to work when we are born, 
and never stops until we stand up to 
make a speech. 


Some people make the world . . . 
Others live in it. 

Edna Ferher. 


People and pins are useless 
When they lose their heads.

Canadian Camping 







Fiims of Camp Interest 

The National Film Board has a new 
moving picture, “The Longhouse Peo¬ 
ple”, which was photographed in colour 
OQ the Brantford Reserve with the full 
co-operation of the tribal leaders, and 
%diich depicts the life, religious cere¬ 
monials, dances, healing ceremonies and 
rribal councils of these fellow Canadi¬ 
ans. Some of them still hold to ancient 
beliefs and customs, and nearly all of 
them feel kinship with the traditions of 
their ancestoi^, even though they live 
and work in the Canada of today. This 
Qm should be of special interest to 
Campers. 

Other films of particular interest to 
campers are “Summer is for Kids,” 
which gives a fascinating picture of 
life at a real camp (to be exact, at 
Pinecrest Camp of the Toronto 
WM.C.A.). Other films are “Canoe 
Trip”, Indian Canoe Man”, and 


“Portage”. Then there are the two 
excellent camp films which are ob¬ 
tainable from the Ontario Camping 
Association office, 52 Avenue Rd., To¬ 
ronto — “A Camper and His Canoe”, 
and “With Paddle and Pack”, 

One of the excellent Arts and Crafts 
films “Animules” was shown at the 
November meeting of the O.C.A. and 
was greatly enjoyed.

Winter 


Winter’s in the North again 
With jewels in her hair^ 

With crystal beads a-shining 
And a spotless gown to wear. 

Her eyes are twinkling like the stars. 

Her cheeks are all aglow, 

And stencilled with blue shadow bars 
Is her mantle of the snow. 

Winter’s in the North again 
With merry bells that chime, 

Echoing through the forest 
The joy of Christmas time. 

The lakes are silvered over, 

Her wand has touched each pane. 

The ski-trails ring with laughter 

For winter’s here .again. —M.S.E.
